purpose: Declare, as data, which fields an object of a given domain carries and
which named relations exist between objects. validate_vault.py READS this
file: the field vocabulary, the permitted values and the required keys are
taken from here, not from Python literals. Adding a field is an edit to
this file, not a code change - which is what issue #4 asked for.
Every entry carries an 'enforced' flag, and the flag is the switch, not a
Since amendment 2026-07-31b this file has TWO readers. validate_vault.py
reads the field vocabulary and the value lists; export_traceability.py
reads the relations, the table bindings and the domain aliases. An entry
flagged 'export-driven' is read by the exporter and by nothing else: it
shapes a report, never a finding that blocks a turn.

enforcement_levels.schema-driven: The validator reads this entry from this file. Changing the entry changes what is enforced, with no code change.
enforcement_levels.validator-internal: The rule lives in validate_vault.py and this file only describes it. Every occurrence names why it was not moved.
enforcement_levels.export-driven: export_traceability.py reads this entry. It shapes the exported graph and the report. The entry itself is never read by validate_vault.py, and the exporter's own findings never become validator findings - the exporter reports, it does not block. A finding never changes its exit code at all; a COVERAGE GAP changes it only where a caller names the gap classes it refuses with --fail-on, which no hook and no session does and this repository's CI does for its own vault (issue #68). Since issue #50 the validator may CONSULT the graph the exporter builds from these entries: requirement coverage does, and the finding it raises is the validator's own (see consistency_rules.requirement-coverage).
enforcement_levels.declared-only: Nothing enforces this. It is declared so that readers - and the undeclared-field check - know the name exists.

domain_aliases.note: A vault written in another language spells its domain folders differently, and every role in this file is written with the English token. This map is the translation, and it is the reason either tool finds requirements in a German vault at all. Since issue #66 both readers resolve roles through one shared derivation, validate_vault.resolve_role_map: the exporter's resolve_roles renders its findings from it, and Vault.roles() feeds the validator's coverage path - req_index, the 'verifies' resolution and the global duplicate scan - so the two tools cannot choose different folders.
domain_aliases.decision: Follow-up 4 of amendment 2026-07-28, unbundled from the convention rollout that blocked it there. It was deliberately not shipped with the validator because requiring 'verifies' in a German evidence domain would have raised 38 ERRORs on a vault that never had the convention. The exporter has no such problem: it reports and never blocks. Issue #66 shipped the coverage half to the validator: req-uncovered, verifies-unknown-req and req-duplicate-global fire in translated vaults, spelled with the vault's own requirement prefix. Issue #115 extended the same reading to the three per-file domain checks and to the requirement-row identifier both readers of 'verifies' compare against. Requiring 'verifies' there stays unshipped - the 38-ERROR rollout is still refused; only checks that read what an author actually wrote gained reach, which is why Vault.fields_for is still keyed by folder abbreviation. See DEC_Per_File_Checks_Follow_The_Role_Map for the tier each of those lands in.
domain_aliases.not_an_alias: TST appears in six homelab and two verdantia allocation-table headers as 'Verifikation (TST)', but no vault has ever had a TST folder - it is a stale column label, not a domain. It is deliberately absent here so the map cannot be read as evidence that such a domain exists.

requirement_id_prefix.rule: The prefix of a requirement row identifier is the abbreviation of THAT vault's requirements domain, not the constant 'REQ'. homelab writes ANF-BAK-001 in its allocation tables and its rows must be indexed under the same string.
requirement_id_prefix.source: the folder abbreviation whose alias resolves to REQ

domain_aliases.unknown_abbreviation: Reported as export-unknown-domain and excluded from the graph. Never guessed: a silent guess is how an export starts describing a vault it did not understand.
domain_aliases.duplicate_role: One role, one folder. Two folders of one vault that mean the same domain - '01_requirements_(REQ)' beside '01_Anforderungen_(ANF)', or '03_architecture_(ARC)' beside '03_Architektur_(ARC)' - are reported as export-duplicate-role, once per excluded folder, naming both folders, both ingestible file counts and the prefix the graph is written with. The kept one stays the first in sorted order, which is a rule and not a judgement: keeping the fuller folder would move every identifier of the export a second time at whatever unrelated edit tips the count, and ingesting both would write every already-translated requirement into the graph twice and report its untranslated twin as unallocated. Sphinx-Needs resolves a duplicate need ID the same way, first wins plus a warning; Doorstop's silent first-wins on load is filed as a defect there (issue #460). Amendment 2026-08-04f, issue #38. Two folders sharing ONE abbreviation are the same finding with a different closing clause: Vault keys its index by abbreviation, so exactly one of them is the vault's, and since amendment 2026-08-04g (issue #42) that one is chosen by pick_domain_dir rather than by readdir - the first in sorted order among the folders holding files of the domain, so a leftover folder carrying nothing but its template never takes it. validate_vault reports the same pair as domain-duplicate-folder (WARN, vault-wide, never blocking) and reads the templates of every folder of the abbreviation, so the files below the folder that lost are not measured against the winner's sections. Measured over eleven vault roots: none carries either shape today, so the fixture in tests/run.sh is the only place it is exercised.

discovery.rule: One packaged schema, read from beside validate_vault.py. There is no per-project override; a vault is checked against the schema shipped with the validator that checks it.
rejected_override: A per-project override at 00_documentation/vault_schema.json was declared by schema 0.1 and is deliberately NOT implemented. It would be a silent off-switch for the blocking gate: the ERRORs that reach the stop gate's blocking set come from check_frontmatter, check_dec_status and check_req_table, which are exactly the checks this file now drives, so a two-line override flipping an entry to 'declared-only' would disable a blocking check from an uncommitted file. That is the same class as 'status: draft' relaxing a rule, which this project rejects outright.

It would also not work where it was meant to. Vault.doc_root is the vault's parent, but a derived project often versions the vault alone - both German production vaults do - so the override path lies outside version control and would not travel with the vault.
A project that genuinely needs different rules forks the skill, which is visible in a diff.
discovery.fallback: If this file is missing or unparseable the validator falls back to a minimal embedded field set and reports schema-unreadable (WARN) once per vault. Validating nothing silently is the failure mode this project has already been bitten by (DECISIONS.md, amendment 2026-07-28).

parts.scope: subsystem token; the same token the subsystem's REQ file carries in parentheses in its filename
parts.number: three digits, local to the (domain, scope) pair

rules: Never reused, gaps allowed - same contract as the REQ row IDs.
REQ files take number 000, reserved for the file itself; REQ table rows use 001 and up, so the file-level and row-level namespaces cannot collide.
Identity lives in the frontmatter, not in the filename: renaming a file does not change its identifier. Wikilinks remain navigation and may be rewritten by the editor.
ADM and INB are excluded: SKILL.md classifies them as not engineering documentation.
identifier.assignment: No registry. The scope token localises the number space; the next free number is found by scanning the vault, following StrictDoc's approach of reading the tree instead of keeping a counter file.

collision_policy.intent: Detect, do not prevent. Two branches can assign the same number and merge cleanly.
collision_policy.today: validate_vault.py reports a collision as id-duplicate (ERROR) and an identifier that was present at git HEAD but is absent from the working tree as id-vanished (WARN). Both are vault-wide checks, so they stay advisory at the stop gate and never block a turn.

scope_resolution.what: The scope token of a REQ file comes from its own id when one is present, and from the parentheses in its filename otherwise.
scope_resolution.consequence: A REQ file carrying an id survives a rename with the identity of its rows intact. A REQ file without an id keeps the historical filename behaviour, which is what every vault predating this scheme relies on.
scope_resolution.residual: The two sources can disagree. The id wins, and id-scope-mismatch (WARN) reports the divergence at the REQ file rather than leaving it to surface as verifies-unknown-req on an unrelated evidence note.

identifier.enforced_detail: The pattern above is NOT compiled from this file at runtime, and the presence of the field is not required. Two separate reasons. (1) Presence: requiring the field would turn every file of a vault predating this scheme into a finding, and only pattern-conforming values take part in any comparison, so two files freshly copied from one template never collide on its placeholder. (2) The pattern stays a Python constant (ID_RE / REQ_ID_RE / ID_EXCLUDED_DOMAINS) because identity resolution runs in module-level functions without a schema in hand, and because it decides which values are compared against git HEAD - a rule that decides what counts as an identity should not be re-readable from the tree being judged. Drift between the two is caught by tests/run.sh, which asserts that the Python constants and the patterns declared here accept and reject the same samples.

code_fences.note: Fenced blocks are restricted where the vault holds pointers rather than copies. The rule is about drift against a named source, not about the three backticks: a copy of a file this repository owns drifts against its original, while a block recording the state of, or a command against, a machine this project does not own is not a copy but a record - ISO 9000:2015 3.8.10, 'document stating results achieved or providing evidence of activities performed', which 'need not be under revision control'.
code_fences.exempt_domains_note: ARC is a map and stores nothing, so no declaration lifts its ban. IMP is where an implementation fact and the observation proving it belong together.
code_fences.record_max_provenance: Measured, not chosen: the smallest genuine script excerpt across both German production vaults has 16 content lines, so 15 is the largest value that still catches every measured copy. Effect at that value, same run pair: homelab code-fence 127 -> 9, PMDE 17 -> 7, template vault unchanged.

declaration.position: any token of the info string, because 23 of 127 blocks in one production vault and 14 of 17 in the other carry no language at all
declaration.value: the name under which the machine is documented - the same name a host-qualified path uses (userver:/etc/...), never an IP, never localhost
declaration.spec: CommonMark 0.31.2: the first word of an info string is typically the language, but 'this spec does not mandate any particular treatment of the info string'. GFM discards further tokens and keeps the language class, so highlighting survives.

codes.code-fence: ERROR - a block past the threshold with no declaration, and every block in ARC
codes.fence-host: ERROR - 'host=' naming no machine; a declaration that names nothing is not a declaration
codes.fence-record: WARN - a declared block past the threshold. Deliberately not silent: nothing can verify that no source file exists, so the exemption stays visible, greppable and countable. It is never an ERROR, because the check cannot distinguish a legitimate record from a disguised copy - Clippy reserves deny-by-default for lints 'free of false positives', Tricorder demands 'no effective false positives' of a blocking check.

code_fences.enforced_detail: The domain lists, the threshold and the attribute name are Python constants (FENCE_BANNED_DOMAINS, FENCE_EXEMPT_DOMAINS, FENCE_RECORD_MAX, FENCE_HOST_RE) for the same reason ID_RE is: they decide what counts as a finding at all, and check_leaks runs per line without a schema in hand. Declared here so the vocabulary has one written home and so a reader finds the reasoning with the rule.
code_fences.not_enforced: That a declared block genuinely has no source file. No rule can establish it from the vault alone; it is the doc-claim grep check (follow-up 2 of the 2026-07-25 decision). Validating the machine name against a declared inventory is the other half and has no home yet - there is no per-project registry location, because the per-project schema override was rejected in amendment 2026-07-28d.

editor_fields.note: Frontmatter keys written by the editor or its plugins. They carry no vault semantics, are never required, and are tolerated in every domain - the undeclared-field check must not report them. Listing them is what keeps that check at WARN-worthy precision instead of flagging a legitimate plugin field as a defect.
editor_fields.provenance: Obsidian Help, 'Properties': tags/aliases/cssclasses are the default properties, publish/permalink/description/image/cover the Obsidian Publish ones. The deprecated singular spellings tag/alias/cssclass are deliberately absent - support for them was dropped in Obsidian 1.9, so a file still carrying one should be reported. A prefix covers the Excalidraw plugin, which writes a whole excalidraw-* family that no enumeration would stay current with.

domain_defaults.note: The vault-wide field vocabulary. It applies to EVERY domain, including the ones 'domains' below does not name - a vault in another language spells its folders ANF/ENT/KMP/SST/TUE/BUN, and reading only the named domains would leave those files unchecked. Per-domain entries in 'domains' merge into this profile attribute by attribute, so a domain that only changes 'required' keeps the type, the values and the finding code declared here. The vault's own SSOT rule applied to its schema: a field shared by every domain is declared once.

field_keys.required: whether a missing key is a finding
field_keys.code: finding code emitted when the value violates its type
field_keys.empty_code: finding code (WARN) when a required list is empty
field_keys.enforced: see enforcement_levels; anything but schema-driven is not checked

domain.note: The value must equal the abbreviation of the folder the file sits in. Declared as a type rather than an enum per domain, because the same rule has to hold for a domain this schema does not name.

status.note: status: draft relaxes no other check.

id.note: Declared vault-wide so that an id is never reported as an undeclared field. The value itself is not checked - see identifier.enforced_detail.

verifies.note: Declared vault-wide, enforced only in TAE (see domains.TAE). A vault in another language carries this field on its own evidence domain - homelab has 37 such files, all with an empty list - and enforcing the rule there would be a convention rollout on a vault that never had the convention, not a defect report. Extending it belongs to the domain-alias follow-up of amendment 2026-07-28.

test-object.note: The objects a TAE note was measured on, as file identifiers. Frontmatter and not prose (amendment 2026-08-05d): a section binding would have to be discovered from template body text, which nothing enforces, and the Test Conditions section carries the setup and the equipment beside the test object. A key is also the only form the blocking layer can check - an identifier naming nothing is a finding, a missing prose annotation never is. Optional everywhere, including TAE: not every note has a physical test object.

REQ.note: Carries the default fields. The identified object in REQ is the table row, not the file; the file's own id reserves number 000.

rows.recognition: A requirement table is recognised by its shape, never by the wording of its header (issue #25, amendment 2026-08-04b): a GFM table - a delimiter row with a header row of the same width directly above it - of at least five columns, whose header carries the template's tokens OR whose rows carry a three-digit number in the second cell, which is the predicate the requirement index uses to decide that a row defines a requirement. A header row is not enforced anywhere and does not survive translation, so keying on its text let one quoted example switch four blocking checks off. The section-title binding table_bindings uses for the exporter was measured and rejected for this: it would leave 34 of the 121 requirement rows on this machine unchecked. In a vault whose requirements role is aliased (ANF), the index applies this predicate under the role map since issue #66, and since issue #115 the row checks read the same folder: what the index reads as a requirement row, a row check reads too. A vault carrying both spellings has both folders row-checked while only one feeds the index, since a per-file check needs no winner and the index does.
rows.unrecognized: req-table-unrecognized (WARN, one grouped finding per file) reports the rows no row check reads: a table the requirement index takes rows from while check_req_table does not, or a REQ file carrying a table wide enough to be a requirement table and not one readable table. WARN and not ERROR because the check cannot tell a revision log or a rubric - both legitimate in a REQ file - from a table that drifted out of readability.
rows.enforced_detail: class_values IS read from here (req-class). The rest - req-nnn, req-duplicate, req-criterion, req-duplicate-global, req-table-unrecognized - stays in Python because it is table structure rather than a value vocabulary. The column count in particular: as data it would be an uncommitted off-switch for four blocking codes, which is what discovery.rejected_override refuses. id_pattern is compared against the validator's REQ_ID_RE by the test suite instead of being compiled at runtime.

DEC.note: The only domain without a frontmatter status: a decision carries its state in the body Status line instead, so that the state and its justification stay in one place.

status.note: Not required, but checked against the same value list when present, so a stray frontmatter status cannot contradict the body Status line unnoticed.

Status.enforced_detail: The value list is read from here. The companion rule - Status 'Superseded' requires a 'Superseded by: [[DEC_...]]' link (dec-superseded, ERROR) - stays in Python: it is a cross-reference requirement, not a value vocabulary. See relations/superseded-by.

TAE.note: The evidence domain. It is the only domain in which 'verifies' is required and checked.

link_annotation.rule: Every cross-domain link in a domain file is annotated with the target's identifier. Because an identifier begins with its domain token, an annotated link carries its own type - no heading is needed to interpret it.

table_bindings.note: A relation table is recognised by the SECTION it sits in, and the section title comes from the project's own 00_*template* file. Files whose name starts with 00_ are excluded from ingestion: templates and READMEs carry the same tables with illustrative rows pointing at objects that do not exist. They are read for one purpose only - to learn what this project's sections are called.

binding_discovery.step_1: Read the domain's own template files. For every H2 section that contains a table, record the section title and the table's header cells.
binding_discovery.step_2: Classify each template table by column count, and for the two four-column ARC tables by whether the last header cell case-folds to the status token: that cell is the one word which is spelled identically in every corpus measured (English 'Status', German 'Status'). The other four-column table is the interface table.
binding_discovery.step_3: In a real file, find the section whose title matches the template's, comparing with the same fold-insensitive rule check_sections uses. ARC takes the first table inside it, because PMDE's templates give two bindings the same section title and only the column count tells them apart. REQ takes EVERY table inside it whose header has the bound column count: requirements are written a layer at a time, and homelab's ANF_Backup_System_(BAK).md holds ten tables under one '## Kontext'. The two rules differ because only REQ has a second gate - a row means nothing unless its second cell carries a requirement number - so a five-column revision history in the same section contributes no row, while an allocation row has no such predicate and would be invented. Column roles are positional in both. Amendment 2026-08-04e, issue #37.
binding_discovery.why_not_the_header: Nothing enforces a header row, and the drift is already in the corpus: homelab's ARC template writes 'Verifikation (TUE)' while six of its fourteen ARC files write 'Verifikation (TST)'. A recognizer keyed on the header accepts 8 of 14 files and 73 of 148 allocation rows. The section title is enforced - check_sections reports a missing or retitled section as a blocking ERROR - and is present in 14 of 14. Measured 2026-07-31.
binding_discovery.header_signature_role: The declared header_signature below is no longer the binding. It is kept as corroboration: a bound table whose header does not match is still ingested, and the divergence is reported as export-header-drift so the vault can be tidied without any row being lost meanwhile.
binding_discovery.unbound_table: Reported as export-unbound-table, and asked differently in the two domains that carry a binding, because they lose rows differently. ARC: a table that sits in no bound section. REQ: a requirement row that did not reach the graph, counted per table and anchored at the first such row. A section-title check cannot ask the REQ question: it would state something false whenever an incidental table merely stands in front of the requirement table in a section that IS declared, and the bound REQ section is the prose section ('## Context', '## Kontext') in all vaults measured, the one most likely to carry a glossary or a revision history. Amendment 2026-08-04d, issue #34. Since amendment 2026-08-04e the bound section contributes every one of its five-column tables, so what the REQ rule still names is a table outside that section and a table inside it whose header is not the bound width. Measured over ten vault roots: 34 rows in one vault carry the first shape, none carries the second, and homelab's 25 findings of this code became 0 because its 78 rows now reach the graph. The check runs before the export-no-scope return and not after, because every REQ file of the vault that carries those 34 rows returns there.
binding_discovery.unbound_table_scope: The seven domains for which this project declares no table binding are exempt, and the exemption is measured rather than assumed: reporting every table they carry adds 663 findings across the same nine roots, including one in the shipped template vault, which is a convention rollout and not a defect report. It is the shape amendment 2026-08-04b rejected as option E for the validator, and the argument carries here even though an exporter finding never blocks a turn: a report nobody can act on trains its reader to skip the section. An empty graph is never silent about a row it could have carried.

arc_allocation_table.qualifier_proven_note: The one value that lets a requirement count as proven. Named here rather than inferred, because 'the last value in the list' and 'the longest one' are both accidents of how the list was written. The German vaults write these five values in English too, so the vocabulary needs no alias.

arc_main_module_table.note: The main-module template's submodule table. It is where an ARC-to-ARC edge is authored, and without it a requirement chain cannot roll up to its top-level module - PMDE nests 26 ARC files five levels deep this way.

req_table.note: Links are read from the justification column alone, never from the row. Two homelab requirement rows carry a wikilink inside the acceptance criterion, and a row-wide scan would turn those into justified-by edges that nobody authored.

table_bindings.enforced_detail: export_traceability.py reads these bindings; validate_vault.py still does not, and no rule asserts that a vault's own tables match the declared header signatures. That asymmetry is deliberate: the exporter produces a report, so a mis-bound table costs a finding in a document, whereas the same rule in the validator would block a turn on formatting drift the author may not own. Residual 4 of amendment 2026-07-28b - reformatting a header row silently removes every relation it carried - is closed by the section binding rather than by a validator rule.

graph.artifact: traceability_graph.mmd, written by export_traceability.py as the 'mermaid' format and part of the default format list. The coverage chain as a Mermaid node-link diagram - the one output of this tool that is a picture rather than a record to read. It carries the diagram source and no Markdown fence, so the same bytes can be embedded in a fenced block and diffed against a fresh run; that diff is what allows README.md to store it at all. Issue #99, DEC-MTH-043.
graph.scope: Three of the nine declared relations: allocates, evidence and verifies - the ones coverage is decided on. Drawing every relation that existed at the time (eight) was measured against the shipped worked example first and produced ten nodes, twenty edges and seven relation words above the fold, in which the only closed cycles are the accidental evidence/test-object pairs rather than the chain a reader was meant to follow. The scope is stated in the diagram's own header and the complete edge set stays in traceability.json and traceability_edges.csv, so the omission is named rather than silent.
graph.identity: Node ids are synthetic: the key sanitised to [A-Za-z0-9_], prefixed 'o_' for a file object and 'r_' for a requirement row, with a counter where two keys sanitise alike. A vault key is not a legal Mermaid id - 'ARC:ARC_Export' and 'REQ_Battery_Monitoring (BAT)' carry colons, parentheses and spaces, and 'end', 'o' and 'x' are reserved words. The two prefixes are load-bearing beyond that: a requirements file may legally carry the identifier of one of its own rows, and one namespace would silently merge the file object with the requirement.
graph.labels: Every label is entity-escaped ('#' first, then " | < > & { } and the backtick), because a label is a record and an allocation status is authored text. A single unescaped '|' ends the edge label and takes the diagram with it, and 'Verified \| Draft' is a spelling the corpus contains. A requirement node also carries its coverage verdict as text - 'proven' or 'not proven' - because the qualifier on the edge shows the word in the cell, and a cell reading 'Verified (Rebuild: Draft)' is qualified and not proven.
graph.determinism: Parallel edges are collapsed on (kind, source, target, qualifier): a requirement allocated in several rows authors one evidence edge per row, which is right in the JSON and is four identical arrows in a picture. Nothing machine- or run-dependent is written - no vault path, no input digest, no generation time - so the file is byte-identical with and without --no-timestamp, which is what lets TUTORIAL.md quote it from a run that carries one.
graph.limits: A large vault yields a diagram nobody can read, and Mermaid refuses a source over 50000 characters. The other five outputs are unaffected and no gate depends on the picture being legible. A vault with no coverage relation at all gets one node saying so, never an empty diagram: an empty diagram is a parse error where a reader was promised a picture.

index.artifact: traceability_index.md, written by export_traceability.py as the 'index' format and part of the default format list. One line per object and per requirement - 'identifier · domain · file · one sentence' - so a session can read what a vault contains once instead of deriving it by search every time. It stays a generated artifact outside the vault, like every other export (STRUCTURE.md); CLAUDE.md names the command rather than a path, because a copy on disk is only ever as fresh as its last run. Amendment 2026-08-05f, issue #53.
index.sentence_section: The section table_bindings.req_table binds, and no second discovery rule. That section is the prose section - '## Context', '## Kontext' - in every vault measured (see binding_discovery.unbound_table), it is enforced by check_sections, and it is already resolved deterministically from the project's own templates. The rejected alternative was an intersection over the H2 titles of every domain template: one template file without the shared title empties it, and the display spelling would have come out of a set, whose iteration order is randomised per process - two runs of one export could then disagree. A vault whose templates declare no requirement table gets no sentences, and the index head says so.
index.sentence_rule: The first block of consecutive prose lines of that section, with headings, table rows, list items, block quotes and fenced blocks stepped over; whitespace collapsed; wikilinks reduced to their display text and their annotations kept; cut at the first '.', '!' or '?' that is followed by whitespace or the end of the text AND whose next non-space character is not a lowercase letter, so 'e.g. the pack' and 'bzw. der Pack' are not cut inside; then capped at 240 characters on a word boundary with an ellipsis. Deterministic and free of judgement - the artifact has to be reproducible. Free text is HTML-escaped when written, because Markdown carries raw HTML and the words are a record, not a document to execute.
index.no_sentence: A file whose bound section carries only tables yields no sentence, and that is not a finding: a requirements file whose context is a table is a legitimate shape, measured across the corpus. The index head counts how many objects have none, so the gap is visible without a report nobody can act on.
index.enforced_detail: export_traceability.py reads this entry; validate_vault.py does not. Nothing about the index blocks a turn.

relations.note: Each kind is authored in exactly one place and in exactly one direction. The reverse direction is computed, never authored - the pattern StrictDoc, Doorstop and Sphinx-Needs all use. Reverse keys follow the Sphinx-Needs '<kind>_back' convention, except where the reverse already has a natural name.

evidence.semantics: A row with several requirements and several evidence notes states that the listed notes together cover the allocation. Which note proves which requirement is answered by 'verifies', not by this relation.
evidence.qualifier_matching: A status counts as the declared value only on an exact match. A cell that begins with a declared value and carries more text - homelab has 19 such rows across 17 distinct spellings, 'Verified (Rebuild: Draft)' among them - is reported as qualified, is NOT counted as proven, and its verbatim text becomes the close-out reason. Neither equality nor prefix matching alone is honest here: equality calls 'Verified (Rebuild: Draft)' unproven without saying why, and prefix matching calls 'Verified (bis 2026-07-25 verletzt)' proven.

verifies.enforced_detail: The field's presence and the format of its elements are schema-driven (domains.TAE). That the referenced REQ rows exist is checked in Python (verifies-unknown-req), because it needs the vault-wide REQ row index rather than a value vocabulary.

justified-by.note: Issue #4 calls this kind 'references'. Named justified-by here after the REQ table column it is authored in ('Source / Justification'), because a bare 'references' would name the mechanism rather than the meaning - every relation in this file is a reference.

contains.authored_in: annotated links in the ARC body, outside the bound tables
contains.subtype_from: domain token of the object identifier
contains.note: The two sources reach different domains, so the domains are declared per source and 'object_domains' is their union, kept for readers that ask what a contains edge may point at. The split is load-bearing: the ARC file template puts a 'Related Modules' bullet in the Context section, and an annotated peer-module link there is navigation, not containment. ARC-to-ARC containment is authored in the submodule table of the main-module template and nowhere else - amendment 2026-08-05d.

test-object.note: Authored in frontmatter since amendment 2026-08-05d. The prose form it declared before was never implemented and could not have been discovered honestly: the Test Conditions section would have to be found from template body text, which nothing enforces, and it holds the setup and the equipment beside the test object.

superseded-by.note: Issue #4 names this kind 'supersedes'. It is authored in the superseded decision, so the subject of the authored line is the OLD decision and the authored direction is superseded-by; 'supersedes' is the computed reverse. Naming it the other way round would reverse the arrow against the other eight kinds, which are all authored subject-first.
superseded-by.enforced_detail: dec-superseded (ERROR) requires the link to be present whenever the body Status is 'Superseded'. The link target is not resolved to a DEC object; that is graph work and belongs to issue #2.

corrected-by.authored_in: DEC body line 'Corrected by: [[DEC_...]]', above the first section heading and below the frontmatter
corrected-by.note: A later decision that overturns a STATEMENT of an earlier one, not the decision itself. It leaves the corrected record's Status untouched - that is the property separating it from superseded-by, and it is the ADR convention: an amended record stays accepted and gains a pointer, a replaced one is superseded. Authored subject-first like the other eight: the pointer sits in the corrected file, so the subject is the OLD decision. An optional short reason may follow the link, as the Superseded by line has always allowed.
corrected-by.enforced_detail: No check of its own, deliberately. A target that resolves to nothing is already a blocking ERROR through link-unresolved, which run_full raises with strict links - measured, not assumed. What stays unenforced: a line carrying no link at all, a line below the first section heading, and every spelling variant ('Corrected-by:', lowercase). A rule for those was designed and rejected - it produced eight false ERRORs in this repository's own method vault and rejected every file freshly copied from the DEC template, whose placeholder is the escaped '\[\[' spelling and therefore carries no link. See DEC_A_Declared_Relation_Without_A_Check_Of_Its_Own. Its siblings dec-status and dec-superseded decide by canonical role since DEC_Per_File_Checks_Follow_The_Role_Map and do fire in a vault that aliases the domain; this relation stays declared-only regardless, for the reason above.

consistency_rules.statement: A requirement is covered when an allocation row names it AND a TAE names it in 'verifies'. An identifier appearing in the prose, in a heading or in a list of open points of an ARC or TAE file is not coverage.
consistency_rules.why: The method's promise is a closed REQ->TAE loop. Until issue #50 the validator decided this with a substring search over whole ARC and TAE files, so a sentence explaining why a requirement was dropped counted as its proof.
consistency_rules.enforced_detail: req-uncovered (WARN), one finding per requirement, at the row that defines it. The 'verifies' half is read from the evidence domain's frontmatter by validate_vault.py itself; the allocation half is read from the graph export_traceability.py builds, because an allocation row sits in the section the project's own ARC template declares and only the binding discovery finds it. Both requirement and evidence domain are resolved through domain_aliases since issue #66, so the rule reaches translated vaults. Where the graph carries no requirement of that identifier - a row outside the bound section, a project whose templates declare no allocation table - the allocation half is not held against the requirement; the exporter names those cases as export-unbound-table and export-no-binding. A vault mid-translation is no longer such a case: index and graph follow one role map, so both read the same requirements folder (export-duplicate-role still names the folder that lost). WARN and not ERROR: the check cannot tell a requirement nobody has verified yet from one whose vault never adopted the 'verifies' convention, which is the same line verified-needs-evidence draws, and vault-wide findings never reach the stop gate's blocking set in any case.

consistency_rules.statement: For every allocation row, the requirements in the 'verifies' frontmatter of the referenced evidence notes should together cover the requirements allocated in that row.
consistency_rules.why: 'verifies' and 'evidence' are separate relations with separate subjects and can disagree without either being wrong on its own.
consistency_rules.note: Reported by the exporter as the coverage gap evidence-disagrees, never by the validator and never under this rule's own id. The rule compares two relations, and neither is extracted until something reads the allocation table into a graph.

consistency_rules.statement: An allocation row with status 'Verified' must carry at least one evidence link.
consistency_rules.note: Reported by the exporter as an informational class, deliberately not as a defect. Measured 2026-07-31 across all six production vaults: 21 findings on homelab and zero everywhere else, and all 21 are rows whose verification is documented as prose ('Preflight in jedem Lauf', 'Vollstaendiger Backup-Lauf 2026-03-23') rather than as a link. Prose verification is thin, but it is not the same defect as an unverified allocation claiming to be verified, and a check that cannot tell them apart is the false-positive class this project refuses in anything that blocks.

consistency_rules.statement: An identifier appears at most once across the vault, and an identifier present in an earlier commit does not silently disappear.
consistency_rules.enforced_detail: id-duplicate (ERROR) for the first clause, id-vanished (WARN) for the second; ADM and INB are excluded from both. The severities differ because the checks differ in kind: a collision is never legitimate, whereas a disappearance can equally be a retirement, a rename or an accidental loss, and no validator can tell those apart.

consistency_rules.statement: A frontmatter key is either declared for its domain, or declared as an editor field, or it is reported.
consistency_rules.why: A mistyped key is the one defect class that fails completely silently: the field looks present and takes effect nowhere.
consistency_rules.enforced_detail: frontmatter-undeclared (WARN), one grouped finding per file listing the unknown keys. WARN and not ERROR because the check cannot distinguish a typo from a deliberate plugin field - Clippy reserves its deny-by-default correctness group for lints free of false positives and files anything that might be intentional under warn-level suspicious, and Tricorder requires a blocking check to produce no effective false positives. Measured cost when introduced: zero findings on the template vault and on both German production vaults.

untyped_links.note: Links that remain navigation in the worked example and are deliberately not relation edges. Listed so the gap is visible rather than implied.
items: Links from a domain file to a 00_ README or template (documentation pointers).
Links inside prose in a Context section that repeat a relation already authored elsewhere in the same file.
